title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: After everything Napoleon had said to him — those bursts of anger and the last coldly spoken words: "I will detain you no longer, General; you shall receive my letter" — Balashev felt convinced that Napoleon would not wish to see him again and would even avoid another meeting with him, an insulted envoy, especially after he had witnessed Napoleon's unseemly outburst. But to his surprise, Balashev received through Duroc an invitation to dine with the Emperor that day.
Bessieres, Caulaincourt, and Berthier were present at that dinner.

Napoleon greeted Balashev cheerfully and warmly. He showed no sign of embarrassment or self-reproach on account of his outburst that morning. On the contrary, he tried to put Balashev at ease. It was evident that he had long been convinced it was impossible for him to make a mistake, and that in his mind whatever he did was right — not because it aligned with any idea of right and wrong, but simply because he did it.

The Emperor was in very good spirits after his ride through Vilna, where crowds of people had rapturously greeted and followed him. From all the windows of the streets through which he rode, rugs, flags, and his monogram were displayed, and the Polish ladies waved their handkerchiefs as they welcomed him.

At dinner, having placed Balashev beside him, Napoleon not only treated him warmly but behaved as if Balashev were one of his own courtiers, one of those who sympathized with his plans and ought to rejoice at his success. In the course of conversation he mentioned Moscow and questioned Balashev about the Russian capital — not merely as an interested traveler asks about a new city he intends to visit, but as if convinced that Balashev, as a Russian, must be flattered by his curiosity.
"How many inhabitants are there in Moscow? How many houses? Is it true that Moscow is called 'Holy Moscow'? How many churches are there in Moscow?" he asked.
And receiving the reply that there were more than two hundred churches, he remarked:
"Why such a large number of churches?"
"The Russians are very devout," replied Balashev.
"But a large number of monasteries and churches is always a sign of a people's backwardness," said Napoleon, turning to Caulaincourt for appreciation of this remark.
Balashev respectfully ventured to disagree with the French Emperor.
"Every country has its own character," said he.
"But nowhere in Europe is there anything like that," said Napoleon.
"I beg your Majesty's pardon," returned Balashev, "besides Russia there is Spain, where there are also many churches and monasteries."

This reply of Balashev's, which hinted at the recent defeats of the French in Spain, was much appreciated when he told it at Alexander's court, but was not much appreciated at Napoleon's dinner, where it passed unnoticed.

The disinterested and puzzled faces of the marshals showed that they were confused as to what Balashev's tone was implying. "If there's a point, we don't see it, or it's not at all witty," their expressions seemed to say. So little was his remark appreciated that Napoleon didn't notice it at all and naively asked Balashev through what towns the direct road from there to Moscow passed. Balashev, who was alert throughout the dinner, replied that just as "all roads lead to Rome," so all roads lead to Moscow: there were many roads, and "among them the road through Poltava, which Charles XII chose." Balashev involuntarily flushed with pleasure at the cleverness of this reply, but hardly had he uttered the word "Poltava" before Caulaincourt began talking about the terrible condition of the road from Petersburg to Moscow and his Petersburg memories.

After dinner they went to drink coffee in Napoleon's study, which four days before had been Emperor Alexander's. Napoleon sat down, toying with his Sevres coffee cup, and motioned Balashev to a chair beside him.

Napoleon was in that well-known after-dinner mood which, more than any reasoned cause, makes a man contented with himself and inclined to view everyone as his friend. It seemed to him that he was surrounded by people who adored him, and he felt sure that after his dinner, Balashev too was his friend and admirer. Napoleon turned to him with a pleasant, though slightly ironic, smile.

"They tell me this is the room the Emperor Alexander occupied? Strange, isn't it, General?" he said, obviously not doubting that this remark would please his listener, since it proved his, Napoleon's, superiority over Alexander.
Balashev made no reply and bowed his head in silence.

"Yes. Four days ago in this room, Wintzingerode and Stein were deliberating," continued Napoleon with the same mocking and self-confident smile. "What I can't understand," he went on, "is that the Emperor Alexander has surrounded himself with my personal enemies. That I do not... understand. Has he not considered that I might do the same?" and he turned inquiringly to Balashev, and this thought evidently brought him back to the anger of that morning, which was still fresh.

"And let him know that I will do it!" said Napoleon, rising and pushing his cup aside. "I'll drive all his Wurttemberg, Baden, and Weimar relatives out of Germany... Yes, I'll drive them out. Let him prepare a refuge for them in Russia!"

Balashev bowed his head with an air that said he would like to take his leave and was only listening because he had no choice. Napoleon didn't notice this expression; he treated Balashev not as an envoy from his enemy, but as a man now fully devoted to him who should rejoice at his former master's humiliation.

"And why has the Emperor Alexander taken command of the armies? What's the good of that? War is my profession, but his business is to reign, not to command armies! Why has he taken on such a responsibility?"

Again Napoleon brought out his snuffbox, paced several times up and down the room in silence, and then suddenly and unexpectedly went up to Balashev and, with a slight smile, as confidently, quickly, and simply as if he were doing something not merely important but pleasing to Balashev, raised his hand to the forty-year-old Russian general's face and, taking him by the ear, pulled it gently, smiling with his lips only.
To have one's ear pulled by the Emperor was considered the greatest honor and mark of favor at the French court.

"Well, admirer and courtier of the Emperor Alexander, why don't you say anything?" said he, as if it were ridiculous, in his presence, to be the admirer and courtier of anyone but himself, Napoleon. "Are the horses ready for the general?" he added, with a slight inclination of his head in reply to Balashev's bow. "Let him have mine — he has a long way to go!"
The letter taken by Balashev was the last Napoleon sent to Alexander. Every detail of the interview was communicated to the Russian monarch, and the war began...
